\section{Definitions}

Throughout, $p$ denotes a fixed prime and all polynomials have integer
coefficients unless stated otherwise. We write $\F_p = \Z/p\Z$.

\begin{definition}[Content and primitive part]
The \emph{content} $\cont(f)$ of $f \in \Z[X]$ is the nonnegative greatest common
divisor of its coefficients. Every nonzero $f$ factors uniquely as $f = \cont(f)
\cdot \pp(f)$, where the \emph{primitive part} $\pp(f)$ has content $1$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[$p$-adic valuation]
For a nonzero integer $n$, $v_p(n)$ is the largest exponent $e$ with $p^e \mid n$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Reduction mod $p$]
The reduction $\overline{(\cdot)} : \Z[X] \to \F_p[X]$ applies the coefficient map
$\Z \to \F_p$ termwise. It is a ring homomorphism, so $\overline{fg} =
\overline{f}\,\overline{g}$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The $\mu$-invariant]
For nonzero $f$, $\mu_p(f) := v_p\big(\cont(f)\big)$. Equivalently, $\mu_p(f) =
\min_i v_p(a_i)$ where $f = \sum_i a_i X^i$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[The $\lambda$-invariant]
For nonzero $f$, $\lambda_p(f) := \trdeg\big(\overline{\pp(f)}\big)$, the
\emph{trailing degree} of the reduced primitive part, i.e.\ the least index $i$
for which the $i$-th coefficient of $\overline{\pp(f)}$ is nonzero.
\end{definition}

\begin{remark}
The definition of $\lambda_p$ requires that $\overline{\pp(f)} \ne 0$; this is
Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero}. $\mu_p$ records the arithmetic depth of divisibility by
$p$, while $\lambda_p$ records a combinatorial/geometric feature of the mod-$p$
reduction.
\end{remark}

\section{Preliminary lemmas}

\begin{lemma}[Reduced primitive parts are nonzero] \label{lem:nonzero}
For every nonzero $f \in \Z[X]$, $\overline{\pp(f)} \ne 0$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Suppose $\overline{\pp(f)} = 0$. Then every coefficient of $\pp(f)$ is divisible
by $p$, so the constant polynomial $p$ divides $\pp(f)$ in $\Z[X]$. Because
$\pp(f)$ is primitive, any constant dividing it must be a unit; but $p \ge 2$ is
not a unit of $\Z$, a contradiction. Hence the reduction is nonzero, and
$\lambda_p(f)$ is well defined.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Gauss's Lemma] \label{lem:gauss}
For nonzero $f, g$, $\cont(fg) = \cont(f)\cont(g)$ up to sign, and consequently
$\pp(fg) = \pp(f)\pp(g)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{lemma}[Trailing degree is additive over a domain] \label{lem:trdeg}
If $R$ is an integral domain and $u, v \in R[X]$ are nonzero, then $\trdeg(uv) =
\trdeg(u) + \trdeg(v)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Writing $u = X^a u_0$, $v = X^b v_0$ with $u_0, v_0$ having nonzero constant term,
the product is $X^{a+b} u_0 v_0$; the constant term of $u_0 v_0$ is the product of
the two constant terms, nonzero because $R$ is a domain. Hence $\trdeg(uv) = a +
b$.
\end{proof}

\section{The central bridge: additivity and the monoid homomorphism}

\begin{theorem}[Additivity of the invariants] \label{thm:add}
For nonzero $f, g \in \Z[X]$,
\[
  \mu_p(fg) = \mu_p(f) + \mu_p(g), \qquad
  \lambda_p(fg) = \lambda_p(f) + \lambda_p(g).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For $\mu$: by Lemma~\ref{lem:gauss}, $\cont(fg) = \cont(f)\cont(g)$ up to sign,
and $v_p$ is additive on products of nonzero integers; hence $\mu_p(fg) =
v_p(\cont f) + v_p(\cont g)$. For $\lambda$: again by Lemma~\ref{lem:gauss},
$\pp(fg) = \pp(f)\pp(g)$, and reduction is multiplicative, so
$\overline{\pp(fg)} = \overline{\pp(f)}\,\overline{\pp(g)}$. Both factors are
nonzero by Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero}, and $\F_p[X]$ is a domain, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:trdeg} gives additivity of the trailing degree.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Values at the identity] \label{prop:one}
$\mu_p(1) = 0$ and $\lambda_p(1) = 0$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The content of $1$ is $1$, whose $p$-adic valuation is $0$. The primitive part of
$1$ is $1$, whose reduction is the constant $1 \in \F_p[X]$, of trailing degree
$0$.
\end{proof}

We now assemble additivity into a single homomorphism. The nonzero elements of the
domain $\Z[X]$ form a multiplicative monoid, denoted $\Z[X]^{\bullet}$. Give $\N
\times \N$ its additive monoid structure with identity $(0,0)$.

\begin{theorem}[The Iwasawa invariant pair is a monoid homomorphism] \label{thm:hom}
The map
\[
  \Phi_p : \Z[X]^{\bullet} \longrightarrow (\N \times \N, +), \qquad
  \Phi_p(f) = \big(\mu_p(f), \lambda_p(f)\big),
\]
is a monoid homomorphism: $\Phi_p(1) = (0,0)$ and $\Phi_p(fg) = \Phi_p(f) +
\Phi_p(g)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Coordinatewise, $\Phi_p(1) = (0,0)$ by Proposition~\ref{prop:one}, and $\Phi_p(fg)
= \Phi_p(f) + \Phi_p(g)$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:add}.
\end{proof}

\begin{remark}
Theorem~\ref{thm:hom} is the precise sense in which $(\mu, \lambda)$ is a
valuation-type object: an additive invariant of a multiplicative structure. It
bridges number theory with the algebra of ordered monoids and valuations. The
monoid $\N \times \N$ is generated by the images of the two elementary
polynomials: $\Phi_p(p) = (1,0)$ and $\Phi_p(X) = (0,1)$.
\end{remark}

\section{$\lambda$ as an order of vanishing}

\begin{theorem}[$\lambda$ is the root multiplicity at the origin] \label{thm:rootmult}
For nonzero $f$,
\[
  \lambda_p(f) = \mult_{0}\big(\overline{\pp(f)}\big),
\]
the multiplicity of $0$ as a root of the reduced primitive part.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
For any nonzero polynomial $u$ over a field, the multiplicity of $0$ as a root
equals the largest $m$ with $X^m \mid u$, which is exactly the trailing degree of
$u$. Applying this to $u = \overline{\pp(f)}$ (nonzero by
Lemma~\ref{lem:nonzero}) identifies $\lambda_p(f)$ with $\mult_0(u)$.
\end{proof}

This is a genuine cross-theory bridge: the Iwasawa $\lambda$-invariant, an
arithmetic datum, coincides with a local algebro-geometric multiplicity.

\section{Monotonicity under divisibility}

\begin{theorem}[Monotonicity under divisibility] \label{thm:dvd}
If $f \mid g$ and $g \ne 0$, then $\mu_p(f) \le \mu_p(g)$ and $\lambda_p(f) \le
\lambda_p(g)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Write $g = f h$. Since $g \ne 0$, both $f$ and $h$ are nonzero. By additivity
(Theorem~\ref{thm:add}), $\mu_p(g) = \mu_p(f) + \mu_p(h) \ge \mu_p(f)$ because
$\mu_p(h) \ge 0$; identically for $\lambda$.
\end{proof}

Monotonicity under divisibility is the hallmark of a valuation: $\Phi_p$
transports the divisibility preorder on $\Z[X]^{\bullet}$ to the product order on
$\N \times \N$.

\section{Finite-product formulas}

\begin{theorem}[Products become sums] \label{thm:prod}
Let $\{f_i\}_{i \in s}$ be a finite family of nonzero polynomials indexed by a
finite set $s$. Then
\[
  \mu_p\!\left(\prod_{i \in s} f_i\right) = \sum_{i \in s} \mu_p(f_i), \qquad
  \lambda_p\!\left(\prod_{i \in s} f_i\right) = \sum_{i \in s} \lambda_p(f_i).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
Induction on the finite index set. The empty product is $1$, with both invariants
$0$ (Proposition~\ref{prop:one}). For the inductive step, split off one factor,
apply Theorem~\ref{thm:add} --- the remaining product is nonzero as a product of
nonzero elements of a domain --- and use the inductive hypothesis.
\end{proof}

\section{The Matsuno twist factor and its iteration}

\begin{definition}[Twist factor]
For $c, k \in \N$, the \emph{Matsuno-type twist factor} is the monomial
\[
  T_{c,k} := p^{\,k}\, X^{\,c\,k} \in \Z[X].
\]
\end{definition}

Using the atoms of the grid one has $\mu_p(p^k) = k$, $\lambda_p(p^k) = 0$,

\[
  \mu_p(T_{c,k}) = k, \qquad \lambda_p(T_{c,k}) = c\,k.
\]

\begin{theorem}[Iterated Matsuno twist] \label{thm:twist}
Let $f \ne 0$ and let $\{(c_i, k_i)\}_{i \in s}$ be a finite family of parameters.
Then
\[
  \lambda_p\!\left(f \cdot \prod_{i \in s} T_{c_i, k_i}\right)
  = \lambda_p(f) + \sum_{i \in s} c_i \, \mu_p\!\big(T_{c_i, k_i}\big).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}[Proof sketch]
The product of twist factors is nonzero, so by Theorems~\ref{thm:add}
and~\ref{thm:prod},
\[
  \lambda_p\!\left(f \cdot \prod_i T_{c_i,k_i}\right)
  = \lambda_p(f) + \sum_i \lambda_p(T_{c_i,k_i}).
\]
Substitute $\lambda_p(T_{c_i,k_i}) = c_i k_i$ and $\mu_p(T_{c_i,k_i}) = k_i$, so
that $\lambda_p(T_{c_i,k_i}) = c_i \mu_p(T_{c_i,k_i})$, giving the stated weighted
sum.
\end{proof}

from __future__ import annotations

from math import gcd
from functools import reduce as _reduce
from typing import List, Tuple


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Basic polynomial arithmetic over the integers                              #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Poly = List[int]


def trim(f: Poly) -> Poly:
    """Remove trailing (high-degree) zero coefficients; keep [0] for the zero poly."""
    g = list(f)
    while len(g) > 1 and g[-1] == 0:
        g.pop()
    return g


def is_zero(f: Poly) -> bool:
    return all(c == 0 for c in f)


def poly_mul(f: Poly, g: Poly) -> Poly:
    """Multiply two integer polynomials."""
    if is_zero(f) or is_zero(g):
        return [0]
    out = [0] * (len(f) + len(g) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(f):
        for j, b in enumerate(g):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return trim(out)


def poly_prod(polys: List[Poly]) -> Poly:
    """Product of a finite family of polynomials."""
    return _reduce(poly_mul, polys, [1])


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Content, primitive part, and p-adic valuation                              #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def content(f: Poly) -> int:
    """Content of f: the (nonnegative) gcd of all coefficients."""
    return _reduce(gcd, (abs(c) for c in f), 0)


def prim_part(f: Poly) -> Poly:
    """Primitive part of f: f divided by its content."""
    c = content(f)
    if c == 0:
        return [0]
    return trim([a // c for a in f])


def padic_val_int(p: int, n: int) -> int:
    """The p-adic valuation of a nonzero integer n."""
    if n == 0:
        raise ValueError("p-adic valuation of 0 is undefined here")
    n = abs(n)
    v = 0
    while n % p == 0:
        n //= p
        v += 1

# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  Basic polynomial arithmetic over the integers                              #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

Poly = List[int]


def trim(f: Poly) -> Poly:
    """Remove trailing (high-degree) zero coefficients; keep [0] for the zero poly."""
    g = list(f)
    while len(g) > 1 and g[-1] == 0:
        g.pop()
    return g


def is_zero(f: Poly) -> bool:
    return all(c == 0 for c in f)


def poly_mul(f: Poly, g: Poly) -> Poly:
    """Multiply two integer polynomials."""
    if is_zero(f) or is_zero(g):
        return [0]
    out = [0] * (len(f) + len(g) - 1)
    for i, a in enumerate(f):
        for j, b in enumerate(g):
            out[i + j] += a * b
    return trim(out)

    """Product of a finite family of polynomials."""
    return _reduce(poly_mul, polys, [1])

    """Content of f: the (nonnegative) gcd of all coefficients."""
    return _reduce(gcd, (abs(c) for c in f), 0)

    """Primitive part of f: f divided by its content."""
    c = content(f)

    """The p-adic valuation of a nonzero integer n."""
    if n == 0:

    n = abs(n)

    while n % p == 0:

    return padic_val_int(p, content(f))

def lambda_inv(p: int, f: Poly) -> int:
    """The Iwasawa lambda-invariant: the trailing degree of the mod-p reduction
    of the primitive part of f (the first index with a nonzero reduced coefficient).
    """
    r = reduce_mod_p(p, prim_part(f))
    for i, c in enumerate(r):
        if c != 0:
            return i
    raise ValueError("reduction of a primitive polynomial should be nonzero")


def root_multiplicity_at_zero(p: int, f: Poly) -> int:
    """Order of vanishing at 0 of the mod-p reduction of the primitive part:
    the largest m with X^m dividing the reduced primitive part.
    """
    r = reduce_mod_p(p, prim_part(f))
    m = 0
    while m < len(r) and r[m] == 0:
        m += 1
    return m


# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #
#  The Matsuno twist factor  p^k * X^(c k)                                     #
# --------------------------------------------------------------------------- #

def twist_factor(p: int, c: int, k: int) -> Poly:
    """The modelled quadratic-twist factor  p^k * X^(c*k)."""
    poly = [0] * (c * k + 1)
    poly[c * k] = p ** k
    return poly

def show(title: str) -> None:
    print("\n" + "=" * 68)
    print(title)
    print("=" * 68)


def demo_additivity() -> None:
    show("1.  Additivity of mu and lambda under multiplication")
    p = 3
    f = [3, 0, 6]          # 3 + 6 X^2  = 3 * (1 + 2 X^2)
    g = [0, 9, 9]          # 9 X + 9 X^2 = 9 X * (1 + X)
    fg = poly_mul(f, g)
    print(f"p = {p}")
    print(f"f  = {f},   mu={mu_inv(p, f)}, lambda={lambda_inv(p, f)}")
    print(f"g  = {g},   mu={mu_inv(p, g)}, lambda={lambda_inv(p, g)}")
    print(f"fg = {fg},  mu={mu_inv(p, fg)}, lambda={lambda_inv(p, fg)}")
    assert mu_inv(p, fg) == mu_inv(p, f) + mu_inv(p, g)
    assert lambda_inv(p, fg) == lambda_inv(p, f) + lambda_inv(p, g)
    print("  mu(fg)  = mu(f)  + mu(g)      verified")
    print("  lam(fg) = lam(f) + lam(g)     verified")


def demo_homomorphism() -> None:
    show("2.  The pair (mu, lambda) as a monoid homomorphism")
    p = 5
    polys = [[5, 0, 10], [0, 0, 1], [25, 5]]
    prod = poly_prod(polys)
    lhs = (mu_inv(p, prod), lambda_inv(p, prod))
    rhs = (
        sum(mu_inv(p, f) for f in polys),
        sum(lambda_inv(p, f) for f in polys),
    )
    print(f"p = {p}")
    for f in polys:
        print(f"  f = {f}: (mu, lam) = ({mu_inv(p, f)}, {lambda_inv(p, f)})")
    print(f"  (mu, lam) of the product      = {lhs}")
    print(f"  sum of (mu, lam) over factors = {rhs}")
    assert lhs == rhs
    print("  homomorphism identity verified")


def demo_divisibility() -> None:
    show("3.  Monotonicity under divisibility")
    p = 2
    f = [2, 0, 2]          # 2 + 2 X^2
    h = [0, 4, 1]          # 4 X + X^2
    g = poly_mul(f, h)     # f divides g
    print(f"p = {p};  f | g")
    print(f"  f: (mu, lam) = ({mu_inv(p, f)}, {lambda_inv(p, f)})")
    print(f"  g: (mu, lam) = ({mu_inv(p, g)}, {lambda_inv(p, g)})")
    assert mu_inv(p, f) <= mu_inv(p, g)
    assert lambda_inv(p, f) <= lambda_inv(p, g)
    print("  mu(f) <= mu(g)  and  lam(f) <= lam(g)   verified")


def demo_root_multiplicity() -> None:
    show("4.  lambda equals the order of vanishing at 0")
    p = 7
    for f in [[7, 0, 0, 3], [0, 0, 14, 7, 2], [1, 7, 49]]:
        lam = lambda_inv(p, f)
        rm = root_multiplicity_at_zero(p, f)
        print(f"  f = {f}: lambda = {lam}, rootMult_0 = {rm}")
        assert lam == rm
    print("  lambda = rootMultiplicity at 0   verified")


def demo_twist() -> None:
    show("5.  The Matsuno twist factor and iterated twist")
    p = 2
    print(f"p = {p}")
    for c, k in [(2, 3), (1, 4), (3, 2)]:
        t = twist_factor(p, c, k)
        print(f"  twist(c={c}, k={k}) = p^{k} X^{c*k}: "
              f"mu = {mu_inv(p, t)} (=k), lambda = {lambda_inv(p, t)} (=c*k)")
        assert mu_inv(p, t) == k
        assert lambda_inv(p, t) == c * k

    f = [1, 0, 3]          # nonzero base characteristic element
    cs, ks = [2, 1, 3], [3, 4, 2]
    twists = [twist_factor(p, c, k) for c, k in zip(cs, ks)]
    twisted = poly_prod([f] + twists)
    lhs = lambda_inv(p, twisted)
    rhs = lambda_inv(p, f) + sum(c * mu_inv(p, t) for c, t in zip(cs, twists))
    print(f"  lambda(f * prod twists)                 = {lhs}")
    print(f"  lambda(f) + sum c_i * mu(twist_i)       = {rhs}")
    assert lhs == rhs
    print("  iterated Matsuno twist formula verified")


def main() -> None:
    demo_additivity()
    demo_homomorphism()
    demo_divisibility()
    demo_root_multiplicity()
    demo_twist()
    print("\nAll demonstrations passed.\n")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
